news_drafts.headline: Havering provisionally agreed for £77m of exceptional financial support; borrowing need forecast at £117.2m
news_drafts.lead:
Havering Council's Audit Committee on 24 November received papers showing that the government has provisionally agreed £77m of exceptional financial support for the council. Exceptional financial support is permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending. The council's Annual Governance Statement for 2025/26 says its application was provisionally agreed at £77m by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government in February 2026.

The statement sets that figure against a remaining 2026/27 budget gap of £77m in a worst-case scenario and £65.9m in a mid-case scenario. It says £10m of savings have been identified for 2026/27 to help close the gap, and that budgets will be allocated within the mid-case scenario. It also says the 2025/26 outturn is an improvement on the assumptions used to set the 2026/27 budget.

The council's half-year treasury management review reports the capital financing requirement for exceptional financial support at £66.6m at 31 March 2026. The capital financing requirement is the total a council has spent on long-lived assets, or in this case support, that it has not yet paid for, in effect its underlying need to borrow. It is forecast at £117.2m at 31 March 2027, from the sixth-month forecast. The council's treasury management strategy statement had estimated £161.4m for that date. The paper reports the figures in its prudential indicator table and does not explain the change.

news_drafts.headline: Havering forecasts £54.2m of exceptional financial support for 2026/27 against £77m agreed
news_drafts.lead:
Havering Council forecasts it will need £54.2m of exceptional financial support in 2026/27, against £77m agreed in its budget, a reduction of £22.8m. The support is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. A cabinet report for 11 November, on the third monitoring period, lists an £11.1m worst-case contingency now unlikely to be needed and £10.1m of ongoing benefit from the 2025/26 outturn. Service budgets are forecast to overspend by £7.1m, offset by corporate budgets.

For 2025/26 the council had agreed £88m of support on a worst-case basis, and the outturn was £37.7m. The council says it will need support again in 2027/28 and will confirm the amount after the December provisional settlement. It has received £6.75m from a £91m one-off transformation grant, from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, for councils receiving such support: £3.06m in 2026/27 and £3.69m in 2027/28. Cabinet is asked to agree its use on spend-to-save projects, with proposed investment of £3.010m in 2027/28 and £3.740m in 2028/29, and full-year ongoing savings of £6.855m.

The medium-term financial strategy assumes the borrowing carries 5% interest and is repaid over 20 years. The paper estimates each £10m costs about £1m a year. Cumulative financing costs of previous years' support reach £17.7m by 2028/29, which is 39% of that year's estimated annual deficit of £44.9m, up from 8% in 2025/26.

news_drafts.headline: Havering auditor EY raises accounts materiality to £13.2m from £8.0m as support risk eases
news_drafts.lead:
Havering's external auditor, the accountancy firm EY, has raised the level at which errors in the council's accounts count as significant from £8.0m to £13.2m. The change is set out in EY's risk assessment dated 10 August 2026, presented to the Audit Committee on 13 October. An external audit is an independent check on the council's accounts.

Materiality is the size of error that could change a reader's view of the accounts. The earlier figure of £8.0m, in the auditor's provisional plan, reflected what the paper calls "additional risk associated with the Authority's receipt of Exceptional Financial Support". That is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending, a last resort. The new figure equals 1.5% of gross expenditure, up from 1%.

EY gives its reason: "as the Authority is now in the third year of receiving this support, the initial risk related to this has reduced in relation to readers of the Statement of Accounts, so this supports an increase in our consideration of our materiality". The statement of accounts is the council's formal annual accounts. Two further thresholds follow from the new figure. Performance materiality, the level used when planning audit testing, is £6.6m. Misstatements above £0.66m will be reported to the committee.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Results Report - 12 November 2026
findings.headline: Havering's 2025/26 audit fee variation is still to be determined, following a 7% one-off variation for 2024/25 project costs.
findings.detail: PSAA set a one-off 7% fee variation for 2024/25 to cover additional work rebuilding assurance, on top of a scale fee variation of £122,251 for 2024/25. For 2025/26, a further scale fee variation is proposed, with the total fee shown as TBD.
findings.matters: Fee variations for rebuilding assurance are a cost that every council in the backlog faces, and the mechanism for recovering them through grant is relevant to other councils' budgets.
findings.figures: 7% one-off variation; £31,662 project costs for 2024/25; £122,251 scale fee variation for 2024/25; £464,973 scale fee for 2025/26 code work
findings.quote: decision to incorporate the project change costs into its review of the grant allocation formula in autumn

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Results Report - 12 November 2026
findings.headline: Five moderate internal control observations are open, down from six at 11 February 2026, with one closed and no new matters reported.
findings.detail: Of the observations open at 11 February 2026, one moderate and one low were closed during 2025/26. No new matters were reported and EY identified no significant deficiencies in internal control.
findings.matters: The count and direction of open control observations is a measure of progress that finance directors at other councils use to benchmark their own action plans.
findings.figures: Open at 11 February 2026: 6 moderate, 1 low (7 total); closed during 2025/26: 1 moderate, 1 low; total open: 5 moderate
findings.quote: We have not identified any additional deficiencies in internal control or improvement recommendations as part of our 2025/26 audit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Results Report - 12 November 2026
findings.headline: EY's planning materiality for the audit is £13.2 million, 1.5% of gross revenue expenditure, up from 1% at the provisional stage.
findings.detail: EY raised materiality because the council is now in the third year of Exceptional Financial Support, which EY says reduces the initial risk to readers of the accounts. Performance materiality is £6.6 million.
findings.matters: The change in materiality, tied to the EFS being in its third year, shows how the auditor reads the council's exceptional support position.
findings.figures: Planning materiality £13.2 million; 1.5% of gross expenditure (previously 1%); performance materiality £6.6 million
findings.quote: We have therefore increased planning materiality to 1.5% of gross expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Results Report - 12 November 2026
findings.headline: Havering's borrowings have been rated Substantial assurance for 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26.
findings.detail: EY completed its planned procedures on borrowings and obtained assurance over the closing balance at 31 March 2026. Cash is also rated Substantial for the same three years.
findings.matters: A Substantial assurance rating on the borrowing balance gives lenders and other councils a verified starting point for the debt position.
findings.quote: We have completed our planned audit procedures in this area and have obtained assurance over the closing balance

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Results Report - 12 November 2026
findings.headline: EY's assurance trajectory has the move to a qualified opinion depending on the 2025/26 audit completing all planned procedures, and says a shortfall would delay it by one year.
findings.detail: The trajectory table places a qualified opinion in the period 2026/27 and 2027/28, and an unmodified opinion in 2028/29, subject to the rebuild work programme. EY says the 2025/26 audit is still in progress.
findings.matters: A fixed timetable for moving from disclaimed to qualified and unqualified opinions is what finance directors elsewhere use to plan their own recovery.
findings.quote: with the move to a qualified opinion being delayed by one year.

editorial.headline: Havering's structural deficit forces £37.7m exceptional support; £240m borrowing conversion ahead
editorial.standfirst: July cabinet papers show Havering's structural deficit requiring exceptional support, as £240m internal borrowing converts to external next year.
editorial.body:
Havering's 2025/26 accounts, presented to July's cabinet, reveal structural revenue collapse. The council's net expenditure reached £242.11m against available funding, "necessitating the use [of] Exceptional Financial Support" of £37.7m. This is not a one-off overspend. The council's own papers describe it as "an underlying budget gap" that already requires further exceptional support budgeted for 2026/27.

The deficit masks systemic failure across core services. Within Living Well, Learning Disabilities overspent by £1.95m despite receiving £4.9m additional growth. The council identifies "complexity pressures" as the culprit—spending on high-cost transition cases and client complexity outpacing new resource. Schools have deteriorated sharply: from a £1.86m surplus at the end of 2024/25 to an overall deficit of £0.72m, with 15 schools now in individual deficit totalling £6.3m.

Capital spending has become the council's chronic drag. Outturn was £135.4m against a £163.7m forecast—a £28.4m shortfall the council attributes to "delayed start on site at four schemes approved to start in 2025/26" across Mercury Land Holdings' housing programme. SEND school expansions were hit by "delays in the procurement process and appointment of contractors." Transport for London schemes went undelivered due to "resourcing constraints," leaving grant funding unclaimed. The council requested £125m carry-forward.

Revenue savings delivery collapsed: £1.2m went unachieved, £2.0m delayed to 2026/27.

The 2026/27 outlook will be defined by debt. The council holds £240m of internal borrowing. Papers note "it is highly likely therefore that further new external borrowing will be needed in 2026/27 both to finance that year's capital programme but also to reduce the level of internal borrowing as those funds are needed for other purposes." This conversion will materially increase debt service costs. The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit stands at £69m; a required £6.9m local contribution hinges on DfE SEND Reform Plan approval.
editorial.pull_quote: increasing levels of client complexity, despite adding in £4.9m of growth
editorial.watch_next: The 2026/27 budget setting will formally confirm the external borrowing requirement and DfE SEND Reform Plan approval status.
